notes: Champion Pension Scheme trustees approved voting for Federal-Mogul Chapter 11 plan and Alternate Payout over Let it Run.

enrichment.short_title: Hearn v Bell: Champion Scheme trustees approve Federal-Mogul plan payout
key_facts: Federal-Mogul Ignition (UK) Limited sponsored the Champion Pension Scheme and was in US Chapter 11 restructuring.
Trustees sought directions on voting for the Third Amended Joint Plan and accepting a GBP 11m Alternate Payout.
Actuarial advice showed the payout secured 100% cover for pensioners and 75% for non-pensioners versus uncertain Let it Run outcomes.
Independent trustee Mrs Hearn chose certainty over equities-dependent Let it Run; the court held that exercise of discretion reasonable.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court application by pension trustees for directions on voting and treatment under a US bankruptcy reorganisation plan.
enrichment.outcome: Directions granted approving trustees' vote for the plan, undertaking to support a CVA, and election of the Alternate Payout treatment.
enrichment.ratio: Where trustees exercise discretionary powers on plan options, the court reviews only whether a reasonable trustee properly directed could reasonably make the decision; actuarial certainty may justify rejecting Let it Run.
legal_issues: Whether trustees could reasonably prefer Alternate Payout to Let it Run
Effect of revised Class 7I treatment decoupled from T&N distribution ratios
Relevance of Pensions Act 2004 PPF and financial assistance provisions
linked_authorities: Hearn v Bell [2004] EWHC 2448 (Ch)

confidence.notes: Detailed reasons on trustee discretion and plan mechanics are clearly recorded.

notes: Extradition habeas corpus to Croatia refused; Fernandez standard not met on ethnic prejudice or delay.

enrichment.short_title: Travica v Croatia: extradition habeas corpus application dismissed
key_facts: A Croatian Serb was committed after in absentia murder and arson convictions relating to 1992 events near Knin.
He claimed risk of prejudice at retrial by reason of Serbian ethnicity and that return would be unjust after delay.
Evidence of alibi witness intimidation and weak prosecution history was general and hearsay-heavy.
Laws LJ reviewed improving Croatian war-crimes justice but held the applicant's specific case did not meet the Fernandez threshold.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court habeas corpus application challenging magistrates' committal to await extradition to Croatia.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; extradition not barred under section 6(1)(d) or section 11(3)(b).
enrichment.ratio: Section 6(1)(d) and section 11(3)(b) require a reasonable chance or serious possibility of prejudice or oppression, not class immunity; relief depends on individual circumstances and adequate evidence, applying the Fernandez test.
legal_issues: Whether a Serb facing Croatian war-crime retrial is prejudiced by ethnicity
Construction of detained or restricted in personal liberty under section 6(1)(d)
Whether delay and lost alibi witnesses make return unjust or oppressive
linked_authorities: Fernandez v Government of Singapore [1982] AC 192
Sivakumaran v Secretary of State for the Home Department [1988] AC 958

confidence.notes: Long judgment with clear holdings on each statutory ground.

notes: Competent terminally ill adult; local authority not obliged to continue injunction against assisted travel to Switzerland.

enrichment.short_title: Re Z: assisted suicide injunction discharged for competent vulnerable adult
key_facts: Mrs Z, disabled by cerebellar ataxia, was legally competent and wished assisted suicide in Switzerland.
Her husband proposed to arrange travel; section 2 Suicide Act 1961 would criminalise his assistance.
Black J had restrained removal; psychiatric evidence confirmed capacity and autonomous decision-making.
Hoffmann LJ discharged the injunction, holding the local authority had no duty to seek its continuation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court inherent jurisdiction hearing on injunction restraining removal for assisted suicide after vulnerable-adult safeguarding intervention.
enrichment.outcome: Injunction discharged; local authority not obliged to apply to continue it; duties on vulnerable adults delineated.
enrichment.ratio: A competent adult may decide to end life and the court cannot prohibit that choice; local authority duties to vulnerable adults do not extend to enforcing criminal law by civil injunction where DPP consent governs prosecution and criminal agencies have adequate powers.
legal_issues: Extent of local authority duties when vulnerable competent adult seeks assisted suicide
Whether court should continue injunction restraining criminal conduct
Balance of sanctity of life, autonomy and Article 2 ECHR
linked_authorities: Airedale NHS Trust v Bland [1993] AC 789
Pretty v DPP [2002] 1 AC 800
R (Burke) v GMC [2004] EWHC 1879 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Clear capacity finding and structured analysis of authority duties and injunctive relief.

notes: Limitation decree may be sought in England without existing local claims; Article 11 does not restrict jurisdiction.

enrichment.short_title: Vessel SA v CP Ships: admiralty limitation jurisdiction without prior claims

statutes_considered.title: Convention on Limitation of Liability for Maritime Claims 1976

key_facts: Owners of tug Polago VI and barge Denise sought a limitation decree after a River Plate grounding.
Cargo claims proceeded in Argentina; English shipping lines held Club letters of undertaking up to USD 3m.
Defendants applied to set aside limitation proceedings for lack of jurisdiction absent English claims.
Steel J held admiralty jurisdiction permitted a limitation action before local claims existed; fund constitution is not mandatory on decree.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Admiralty application to set aside limitation proceedings for want of subject-matter jurisdiction.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; court has jurisdiction to grant a limitation decree; standard basis costs awarded.
enrichment.ratio: Article 11 restricts where a limitation fund may be constituted, not whether limitation may be invoked; English admiralty jurisdiction under section 20 SCA 1981 allows a decree even without proceedings in England, and Article 10 permits invoking limitation without a fund.
legal_issues: Whether limitation proceedings require existing claims in the same jurisdiction
Interaction of 1976 Convention Articles 10 and 11 with English procedure
Whether a limitation fund must be established once a decree is granted
linked_authorities: ICL Vikraman [2004] 1 Lloyd's Rep 21

confidence.notes: Short judgment with clear jurisdictional ruling on Convention and statute.

notes: Fatal dock accident; clause 23(iv) excluded contractor indemnity for SCT's own default despite broad clause 22 wording.

enrichment.short_title: Brown v Drake: contractor indemnity clause 23(iv) overrides clause 22
key_facts: Mr Brown was killed at Southampton Docks when struck by a straddle carrier during pole delivery.
Judge found equal negligence of labour supplier Drake and terminal operator SCT and an indemnity in favour of SCT.
Clause 22 required contractor indemnity however caused; clause 23(iv) excepted injury resulting from SCT's act or default.
Court of Appeal held clause 23(iv) prevailed so SCT was not indemnified for its share of liability.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on indemnity and contributory apportionment after county court fatal accident judgment.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on indemnity; equal apportionment upheld; Drake not required to indemnify SCT for SCT's moiety.
enrichment.ratio: Where a contract contains a specific indemnity excluding liability for the proferens's own default, it prevails over a general however-caused indemnity; Canada Steamship three-stage analysis is satisfied by however caused but does not override the later specific clause.
legal_issues: Construction of however caused indemnity under Canada Steamship Lines
Whether clause 23(iv) insurance heading limits its effect as an indemnity
Apportionment between joint controllers of an unsafe dock system
linked_authorities: Canada Steamship Lines v The King [1952] AC 192
Smith v South Wales Switchgear [1978] 1 WLR 165
White v Blackmore [1972] 2 QB 651

confidence.notes: Detailed contractual analysis with unanimous outcome on indemnity and apportionment.

notes: Section 288 challenge to salt-mine waste permission dismissed; EIA contained sufficient risk data.

enrichment.short_title: Kent v SSHD: EIA challenge to Winsford salt cavern waste permission fails
key_facts: Secretary of State granted permission for hazardous waste disposal in rock salt caverns at Winsford after a reopened inquiry.
Local resident challenged the environmental statement as lacking hard data on waste types and risk assessment.
Inspector and multiple authorities had accepted the ES; condition (xii) tied generic waste types to the permission.
Harrison J held the ES was not so deficient as to be no ES at all and PPC could address residual detail.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court section 288 application to quash Secretary of State planning permission for underground waste disposal.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; planning permission upheld; wasted costs order made against claimant's counsel.
enrichment.ratio: An environmental statement need only enable identification and assessment of main likely significant effects; generic waste types and risk scenarios may suffice at EIA stage where parameters are fixed by conditions and PPC provides later controls, and PPC cannot cure a fundamentally unlawful ES but this was not such a case.
legal_issues: Whether the ES lacked Schedule 4 data on waste types and risk
Use of IPPC/PPC regime as surrogate for EIA assessment
Validity of monitoring and chemist conditions
linked_authorities: R v North Yorkshire County Council ex parte Brown [1999] 1 WLR 452
R v Rochdale Metropolitan Borough Council ex parte Milne [2001] Env LR 23
R v Blewett [2003] Env LR 32

confidence.notes: Very long judgment but conclusions at paragraphs 74-87 are explicit.

notes: Spent affray conviction character direction upheld; attempted kidnapping conviction safe; sentence cut to four years.

enrichment.short_title: Mentor v R: character direction fair; kidnapping sentence reduced
key_facts: Appellant convicted of attempted kidnapping after an incident on Walditch Road involving a female complainant.
Defence adduced good character evidence but also a five-year-old spent affray conviction.
Recorder directed jury to balance character evidence against the conviction when assessing credibility.
Court dismissed conviction appeal as safe but reduced six-year sentence to four years as manifestly excessive.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal (Criminal Division) against conviction and sentence for attempted kidnapping.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeal dismissed; sentence appeal allowed; term reduced from six to four years imprisonment.
enrichment.ratio: Where a spent violent conviction is not irrelevant to credibility, a balanced direction referencing both good character and the conviction is lawful under R v Nye discretion; propensity limb of good character direction was not required, and sentence for attempted kidnapping should be below attempted rape levels.
legal_issues: Whether spent affray conviction required full good character direction
Safety of conviction where character direction omitted Vye second limb
Appropriate sentence compared with attempted rape and kidnapping authorities
linked_authorities: R v Nye (1982) 75 Cr App R 247
R v Vye [1993] 97 Cr App R 134
R v Lashley (1988) 10 Cr App R (S) 396

notes: Declarations that Mental Health Act 1983 sections 2 and 29(4) incompatible with Article 5(4) ECHR.

enrichment.short_title: R (MH) v SSHD: section 2 and 29(4) incompatible with Article 5(4)
key_facts: MH, with Down's syndrome, was detained under section 2 but could not apply to the MHRT due to incapacity.
A section 29 nearest-relative application extended detention for many months without MHRT review.
Silber J refused relief; Court of Appeal held Article 5(4) requires equivalent access for incompetent patients.
Declarations of incompatibility made under section 4 rather than reading down the statute.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal human rights challenge to Mental Health Act detention and review mechanisms.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; declarations that sections 2 and 29(4) are incompatible with Article 5(4) ECHR for lack of court reference mechanisms.
enrichment.ratio: Article 5(4) obliges the state to put incompetent patients in the same position as competent patients regarding review of detention; automatic 28-day release is not an adequate substitute where competent patients may apply to the MHRT, and section 29(4) extensions without MHRT access breach Article 5(4).
legal_issues: Whether incompetent section 2 patients need automatic MHRT reference
Whether County Court section 29 proceedings provide Article 5 review
Remedy: section 3 reading down versus section 4 declaration
linked_authorities: Winterwerp v Netherlands (1979) 2 EHRR 387
R (S) v City of Plymouth [2002] 1 WLR 2582
HL v United Kingdom (2004) application 45508/99

notes: Mineral planning Schedule 13 deemed conditions appeal allowed; parties agreed three-month extension to July 2000.

enrichment.short_title: Wirral v Brock: Schedule 13 time extension agreement defeats deemed conditions
key_facts: Brock applied under Schedule 13 to determine conditions for Prenton Quarry mineral permissions before 29 February 2000.
Council treated application as complete on 28 February but later argued environmental statement details delayed time until April.
Correspondence showed both parties worked on a three-month period ending 20 July 2000; Council determined conditions on 17 July.
Court of Appeal held there was a written agreement extending determination time, reversing deemed applicant conditions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal on construction of Schedule 13 mineral conditions application and deemed determination under paragraph 9(9).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; no deemed adoption of Brock's proposed conditions; Council's 17 July determination within agreed extended period.
enrichment.ratio: Schedule 13 paragraph 9(2) sets application content; paragraph 9(10) further-details notices must be timely; the three-month period in 9(9) may be extended by written agreement construed in context, and subsequent conduct showed agreement to run time from 20 April to 20 July.
legal_issues: When a valid Schedule 13 application was made
Whether March 2000 letter was a paragraph 9(10) further-details notice
Whether correspondence constituted written extension agreement
linked_authorities: R v Durham County Council ex parte Huddleston [2000] 1 WLR 1484
R v Somerset County Council ex parte Morris [1999] PLCR 117
R (Wells) v Secretary of State for Transport [2004] Env LR 27

notes: MHRT refusal to discharge section 3 patient on extended leave held lawful; treatment in hospital includes ward rounds.

enrichment.short_title: R (CS) v MHRT: section 3 detention on leave with ward rounds lawful
key_facts: CS, diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia, was detained under section 3 but on extended section 17 leave with AOS support.
MHRT refused discharge in February 2004 citing history of non-compliance and need for phased hospital-linked treatment.
Claimant argued section 3 required in-patient admission and recall powers were disproportionate under Article 5.
Pitchford J held ward rounds and psychology sessions were significant hospital treatment; claim dismissed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court judicial review of Mental Health Review Tribunal decision refusing discharge from section 3 detention.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; tribunal decision lawful and rational; football pools costs order in favour of defendants.
enrichment.ratio: Section 3 detention may include substantial leave where treatment in hospital remains a significant component of the overall plan; following Barking, renewal and recall mechanisms support phased rehabilitation, and section 72 proportionality does not add a separate Article 5 test beyond non-arbitrary domestic law.
legal_issues: Whether section 3 requires actual in-patient residence
Lawfulness of detention mainly in community with four-weekly ward rounds
Need to consider guardianship or supervised community treatment alternatives

R v Barking Havering and Brentwood Community Healthcare NHS Trust [1999] 1 FLR 106
